extracted.intended_audience: Reviewers (current and prospective) for the Journal of Open Source Software (JOSS)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for performing peer review of software+paper submissions to the Journal of Open Source Software, covering reviewer responsibilities, time expectations, conflict-of-interest rules, and procedural practices (filing issues, use of EditorialBot).

rubrics_metrics.name: Developer-friendly expectations / software best practices
rubrics_metrics.description: If the submitting authors have followed best practices (have documentation, tests, continuous integration, and a license) then their review should be rapid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should expect and look for documentation, tests, CI, and an explicit license as indicators of quality and ready-to-review software; absence of these is a reason to give constructive feedback and may slow review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective checklist-based review
rubrics_metrics.description: A JOSS review involves checking submissions against a checklist covering software quality, development practices, and required paper content. This should be objective, not subjective; it should be based on the materials in the submission as perceived without distortion by personal feelings, prejudices, or interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base assessments on the submission materials; avoid letting personal biases influence judgments. Use the provided checklist as the basis for acceptance decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checklist coverage: software quality, development practices, and required paper content
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers check submissions against a checklist covering: software quality, development practices, and required paper content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three topical dimensions are the core areas used to determine acceptability; use them to structure review and to point to specific deficiencies or required changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide clear, constructive feedback to improve submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: For those submissions that don’t quite meet the bar, please try to give clear feedback on how authors could improve their submission. A key goal of JOSS is to raise the quality of research software generally and you (the experienced reviewer) are well placed to give this feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When software or paper falls short, identify concrete, actionable changes (e.g., add tests, improve docs, fix CI) rather than vague criticism; help authors reach the required standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time expectations for reviewers and authors
rubrics_metrics.description: We ask reviewers to complete their reviews in 4–6 weeks, and we generally ask the same commitment from authors: they should respond to your feedback within 2 weeks and complete requested changes within 4–6 weeks, unless otherwise negotiated with the editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a first-pass review within about 2–4 weeks; notify the editor if you need more time. If an author becomes unresponsive, the editor will follow up. Negotiate deadlines with the editor for substantial changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage filing and linking issues in repository issue tracker
rubrics_metrics.description: We encourage reviewers to file issues against the submitted repository’s issue tracker. You can include in your review links to any new issues that you the reviewer believe to be impeding the acceptance of the repository.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When you have completed your review, please leave a comment in the review issue saying so. If the submitted repository is a GitHub repo, mentioning the review issue URL in the submitted repository’s issue tracker will create a mention in the review issue’s history — use these links to document blocking problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use EditorialBot and communicate availability
rubrics_metrics.description: You can also use EditorialBot (our bot) to set automatic reminders if you know you’ll be away for a known period of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be upfront about availability; tell the editor if you require more time. Use EditorialBot reminders to manage known absences so the editor can coordinate the review process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of Interest (COI) policy and disclosure requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A conflict of Interest in peer review is a circumstance that makes you 'unable to make an impartial scientific judgment or evaluation.' JOSS is concerned with avoiding actual conflicts and appearances of conflicts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report present or previous associations with any authors: recent (past four years) collaborators in funded research or work that is published; lifetime for family members, business partners, and thesis student/advisor or mentor; and recent (past year) association with the same organization of a submitter (e.g., being employed at the same institution). If you have a COI, disclose the specific reason to the submission’s editor (or EiC as appropriate). Conflicts may be recorded and waived in some cases (examples given: being one of 2000 authors on a paper, old collaborations whose timelines are distorted by publishing delays). Declare actual, perceived, and potential conflicts; if in doubt, ask the editors.
